title: New restaurant marketing for a strong opening
seoTitle: New restaurant marketing for a strong opening | ROAL
description: Plan local marketing for a new restaurant opening with phone tactics, launch offers, and a simple way to turn calls into orders.
question: How do I do new restaurant marketing for an opening without wasting money?
answer: Focus on the basics that bring calls and first visits: clear listings, a simple opening offer, strong phone handling, and a way to answer hours, menu, and pickup questions fast. Make sure every promotion points people to the same phone number, menu, and address so callers can place an order or get info without friction.
summary: Build a simple opening marketing plan that drives calls, pickup orders, and repeat visits.
intro:
A good new restaurant marketing plan starts with one goal: make it easy for nearby customers to call, order, and find you on day one. Keep your message simple, your hours clear, and your phone covered during the rush.

For an opening, the fastest wins usually come from local search, social posts, launch offers, and a phone setup that can handle real calls. ROAL can help with the phone side by answering questions, taking pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, and sending clean tickets to the kitchen.

sections.h2: What should I fix before I start marketing my opening?
sections.body:
Before you post anything, make sure the basics are ready. People will forgive a small menu, but they will not forgive a wrong phone number, a missing address, or a voicemail that never gets checked.

Use this opening checklist:
- Confirm your name, address, and phone number are the same on your website, maps listing, and social profiles.
- Post your hours, including the first few weeks if they are limited.
- Upload a clean menu with prices and sold-out items removed.
- Decide how calls will be handled during lunch and dinner.
- Write a short opening message for your voicemail and social pages.

A simple phone script helps too. Try: "Thanks for calling. We are open now for pickup and delivery. You can place your order here, or we can answer menu and hours questions." If you use ROAL, it can answer the phone from your live menu and give callers your hours, address, and parking details without you having to repeat them all day.

sections.h2: Which launch channels should a new restaurant use first?
sections.body:
Do not try every channel at once. Start with the places people already use when they want food tonight or want to check if you are real.

A practical launch order looks like this:
1. Your website with menu, hours, address, and a clear call button.
2. Maps and local listings, so people can find directions fast.
3. Social posts that show the food, the storefront, and the opening day.
4. Flyers, counter cards, and neighborhood handouts that point to the same phone number.
5. A launch offer that is easy to understand, like a first-week combo or a pickup special.

If you want a deeper local checklist, see [Apple Maps and Yelp listings for restaurants](/blog/apple-maps-yelp-listings-restaurant). For social content that pushes people to call, [social posts that make people call](/blog/restaurant-social-media-takeout) is the next step. The key is consistency: every place someone sees your restaurant should tell the same story and lead to the same order path.

sections.h2: How do I turn opening interest into actual orders?
sections.body:
Opening interest is nice, but orders pay the bills. Your marketing should make it obvious what to do next: call, order pickup, ask a question, or check if you are busy.

Here is a simple opening-day workflow:
- Put your phone number on every flyer and post.
- Say exactly what you want people to order first.
- Offer one or two easy specials instead of a long list of promos.
- Make sure someone answers questions about the menu and hours right away.
- Keep the kitchen ready for the first wave of calls.

Worked example: say your average pickup order is $28. If 20 callers place orders in a week, that is $560 in sales before repeat business. Plug in your own average order size and your own call volume. The point is not the exact number; the point is to make every call easy to turn into a completed order.

ROAL is built for that phone step. It can take items, sizes, modifiers, notes, caller name, phone number, and ready time, then send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

sections.h2: What should I say in opening offers and phone promos?
sections.body:
A weak offer sounds vague. A strong offer tells people what to order, when to order, and why they should call now.

Good opening promo examples:
- "Grand opening pickup special: one appetizer, two entrees, and two drinks."
- "Call for today’s lunch combo and pickup time."
- "Ask about our opening-week family meal."
- "Order by phone for pickup and get your ready time before you leave home."

Keep the offer easy to explain in one sentence. If the promotion is too complicated, staff will waste time repeating it and callers may give up. Also make sure the offer matches what your kitchen can actually handle. A busy new restaurant does better with one clean offer than with five confusing ones.

If you are planning email or text around the opening, pair the offer with a simple message and a direct phone number. [Email and text marketing for restaurants](/blog/restaurant-email-marketing) has a good framework for that. For quieter nights after opening week, [slow-night promotions that bring calls](/blog/slow-night-promotions) can help you keep the phone moving.

sections.h2: How should I handle phone calls during opening week?
sections.body:
Opening week is when the phone matters most. People call to ask your hours, your address, whether you have parking, what is on the menu, and whether you are too busy to take an order.

Set up your call flow before the first rush:
1. Decide whether all calls forward or only busy and unanswered calls forward.
2. Test the call forwarding from a real phone.
3. Record a short backup greeting for times when staff are tied up.
4. Make sure someone can answer complaint, allergy, and catering questions.
5. Keep a list of menu items that are sold out.

If you need the carrier codes, use [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes), then confirm with your carrier and test with a call. Many landlines and some carriers use *72 to forward all calls and *73 to turn it off. Some mobile plans use different codes for all calls, busy calls, or unanswered calls, so always verify.

ROAL can sit in that front line by answering common questions, taking orders, and passing harder calls to staff with a summary. That is useful when the team is busy and you still want the phone to be covered.

sections.h2: How do I price and measure marketing without overspending?
sections.body:
A new restaurant opening can burn cash fast, so keep your numbers simple. You do not need a giant campaign. You need a small plan that you can track every week.

Use this basic math:
| Item | Example number | What to replace it with |
|---|---:|---:|
| Average order | $28 | Your own average order |
| Orders from opening promo | 25 | Your own call volume |
| Promo sales | $700 | 28 x 25 |
| Delivery app commission | 15-30% | Your own commission rate |
| Phone handling cost | Use your own setup | Your own cost |

This does two things. First, it shows whether your promo is bringing in enough orders. Second, it helps you compare channels. Delivery apps commonly take roughly 15-30% per order, so even a modest pickup campaign can look better if it brings people to your own phone line.

For phone costs, some AI phone tools charge a monthly fee per location whether or not orders come in, while human answering services often bill per minute or per call. ROAL uses a pay-per-completed-order model at $0.90 per completed phone order, with no monthly fee or setup fee. If you want to compare the options, [pricing](/pricing) and [pay per order vs monthly AI phone plans](/compare/monthly-ai-phone-plans) are useful starting points.

sections.h2: What should I do after opening week to keep momentum?
sections.body:
The opening is only the start. After the first rush, your job is to make the restaurant easier to remember and easier to call next time.

Keep doing these simple things:
- Post one or two real food photos each week.
- Update hours and holiday closures right away.
- Watch call history so you know what people ask most.
- Add new FAQs for common questions about parking, wait time, or menu items.
- Refresh your opening offer into a repeatable weekly special.

A useful owner habit is to review what people asked on the phone and turn that into better marketing. If callers keep asking about gluten-free items, parking, or late-night pickup, make those details visible on your site and posts. That reduces friction and helps the next caller act faster.

If you want to test a phone setup before you launch, [build a free test host](/try). You paste your website, Google Maps link, or Name, City, test-call it in the browser, and see how it handles menu and hours questions before you go live.

takeaways: Start with the basics: clear hours, address, menu, and one phone number everywhere.
Use one simple opening offer and point all marketing to the same call to action.
Make phone handling part of the launch plan, not an afterthought.
Track the math with your own average order and call volume, not guesses.
Review common caller questions after opening week and update your marketing from them.

faq.q: What is the best new restaurant marketing for a small opening budget?
faq.a: Start local and keep it simple. Make sure your maps listing, website, and social profiles all have the same name, address, phone number, hours, and menu. Then run one clear opening offer that pushes people to call or order pickup.

faq.q: Should I use delivery apps when my restaurant first opens?
faq.a: They can bring visibility, but they often take roughly 15-30% commission per order. Many new restaurants use them carefully while also pushing pickup and direct phone orders so more of the sale stays with the restaurant.

faq.q: How do I handle phone calls if I’m too busy opening the restaurant?
faq.a: Forward your calls to a system you can control and test it before opening day. ROAL can answer common questions, take pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, and pass allergy, catering, complaint, and manager requests to staff with a summary.

faq.q: What should a new restaurant say on the phone?
faq.a: Keep it short and helpful: "Thanks for calling. We can answer menu and hours questions, or take your pickup order now." If you have a special opening offer, mention it once, then move straight to the order or question.
